abstract: Understanding the obligate relationship between freshwater unionid mussels and the host fish(es) of their larvae (glochidia) is key to the conservation of this generally threatened fauna. A host relationship between at-risk species Hickorynut (Obovaria olivaria) and Lake Sturgeon (Acipenser fulvescens) in Canada has long been presumed based on evidence from laboratory experiments in the United States. This study aimed to make a definitive link in the wild between these two species, while also examining other potential fish-mussel connections in the Ottawa and St. Lawrence Rivers. Using a combination of field collections, morphological and genetic examinations of glochidia from wild-caught fishes, and morphological examination of glochidia from archival specimens from natural history collections, we make a definitive link between these two species for the first time in nature in Canada, with evidence for both natural infestation and natural transformation. This work provides novel methodologies that are widely applicable to studies of mussel-fish relationships and reveals the utility of natural history museum, and other, fish collections for their study.
